```{r}
#| label: chapter-root
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
source(here::here("preamble-packages.R"))
source(here::here("preamble-data.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: packages-header
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
packages_used_callout(rmarkdown::metadata$packages)
```

The Situation Brief works. It pulls fresh data from the API, computes its
own verdict, and renders to a page the Commissioner can read without
opening R. Every question the scenario has asked so far, the town-level
table could answer.

Then, on the incident-command call, you get two you can't:

> "Why do last week's numbers keep changing *after* we've briefed them?"
>
> "And positivity is up — but I'm told most of our testing is rapid
> antigen now. Is that the same eleven percent it was in December?"

Check the table you've been using. It has `number_of_tests`,
`number_of_positives`, `people_tested` — a denominator is in there, and
that's not the problem. The problem is that every one of those is a
**cumulative total as of a report date**. Nothing in it says which lab
ran the test, how many days passed between the swab and the result, which
of those results was a correction to one already counted, or whether it
was a PCR or a rapid antigen test.

Those answers live one level down, in the data the town counts were built
*from*: the laboratory feed. One row per test result, every result, from
every lab in the state. That file does not fit in your laptop's memory,
and this part is about what you do when that happens.

## Meet the lab feed

Public health labs report results electronically — a stream of messages
in a format called **ELR** (electronic laboratory reporting), which
surveillance systems flatten into one very wide table. The book ships a
synthetic version of that feed.

::: {.callout-warning}
## This data is fake

`synthetic-covid-lab-results.csv` is generated by a script. No row
describes a real person, provider, or laboratory — the names, CLIA
numbers, NPIs, and specimen IDs are all invented. What *is* real is the
vocabulary: the LOINC, SNOMED CT, and ICD-10-CM codes are the genuine
published codes, so the shape of the work is the shape of the real job.
See the [Data Library](../data-library/index.qmd) for details.
:::

```{r}
#| label: peek-feed
lab_results <- read_book_data("synthetic-covid-lab-results.csv")

dim(lab_results)
```

Forty-three columns. Here are the ones this part leans on:

```{r}
#| label: peek-columns
lab_results |>
  select(
    specimen_id,
    performing_lab,
    specimen_collection_dt,
    result_dt,
    test_method,
    result_snomed,
    result_value,
    result_status
  ) |>
  head(4)
```

Every row is one test. `result_snomed` is the coded answer —
`260373001` is SNOMED CT for *Detected*, `260415000` for *Not detected*.
`test_method` is the thing the town table never carried.

### The types are already wrong

Before going further, look at what `read_csv()` decided those columns
are:

```{r}
#| label: wrong-types
lab_results |>
  select(result_snomed, specimen_source_snomed, ordering_provider_npi) |>
  sapply(class)
```

Doubles. All three. And `readr` did nothing unreasonable — every value in
those columns is made of digits, so "number" is a perfectly good guess
from the evidence available.

It is still wrong. A SNOMED code is a **label**, not a quantity. Nobody
adds two NPIs together. Treat identifiers as numbers and you eventually
get bitten in one of three ways: a leading zero silently disappears
(`06001` becomes `6001`), a long code loses precision at the far end of
what a double can hold exactly, or someone writes the file back out in
scientific notation and you inherit `2.6e+08`.

The fix is to say so, every time you read the file:

```{r}
#| label: peek-feed-typed
lab_results <-
  read_book_data(
    "synthetic-covid-lab-results.csv",
    col_types = cols(
      result_snomed = col_character(),
      specimen_source_snomed = col_character(),
      ordering_provider_npi = col_character(),
      patient_zip = col_character(),
      .default = col_guess()
    )
  )

class(lab_results$result_snomed)
```

Remember that you had to do that. It comes back in the next chapter.

### Positivity, by method

With the codes as codes, the Commissioner's second question is a
`group_by()`:

```{r}
#| label: positivity-by-method
lab_results |>
  filter(!is.na(specimen_collection_dt)) |>
  mutate(quarter = as.Date(cut(as.Date(specimen_collection_dt), "quarter"))) |>
  summarise(
    tests = n(),
    positives = sum(result_snomed %in% c("260373001", "10828004")),
    .by = c(quarter, test_method)
  ) |>
  mutate(positivity = round(100 * positives / tests, 1)) |>
  filter(quarter >= as.Date("2020-10-01")) |>
  arrange(quarter, test_method)
```

Same headline positivity, split by how the test was run — and the answer
to "is it the same eleven percent" is visible in the columns. That is
ordinary `dplyr`; nothing new. The problem isn't the analysis. The
problem is the file.

## The wall

The snapshot in this book is small on purpose, so the book can render:

```{r}
#| label: file-size
fs::file_size(book_data_path("synthetic-covid-lab-results.csv"))
```

Twenty-five thousand rows. Now look at what the real feed would be. The
town table records how many tests Connecticut had actually run by the end
of the archive:

```{r}
#| label: real-scale
read_book_data("ct-covid-by-town-2026-06-30.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(report_date = lubridate::mdy(last_update_date)) |>
  filter(report_date == max(report_date)) |>
  summarise(tests_statewide = sum(number_of_tests, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Sixteen and a half million tests. One row each, at the width you just
saw, is somewhere north of **ten gigabytes of CSV**.

Here is what `read_csv()` does with a ten-gigabyte CSV on an
eight-gigabyte laptop: nothing good. Usually R grinds for several minutes
and then dies with `Error: cannot allocate vector of size ...`, or your
machine starts swapping and everything — R, your browser, your email —
crawls.

It's worth being precise about *why*, because the reason points at the
fix.

**1. `read_csv()` is all-or-nothing.** It reads the entire file into RAM
before you get a single row back. Ask for three columns out of
forty-three, and it still reads all forty-three. Ask for one month out of
eighteen, and it still reads all eighteen.

**2. In-memory is bigger than on-disk.** A CSV is text. A data frame of
that same text carries per-column and per-vector overhead on top of the
values themselves. Two to three times the file size in RAM is a
reasonable planning figure for a wide, text-heavy file like this one.

**3. Parsing text is genuinely expensive.** Every `2021-02-06T13:28:51Z`
has to be recognized as a timestamp and converted. Every `24.5` has to be
turned from four characters into a double. Multiply by forty-three
columns and sixteen million rows.

**4. A CSV knows nothing about itself.** There is no header block saying
"column 21 is a timestamp, column 40 is a float, there are 16,515,446
rows, and the earliest collection date is 2020-01-15." Every reader has
to work all of that out by reading the data — which means even
"how many rows is this?" costs a full pass over ten gigabytes.

Point four is the deep one. The other three follow from it.

## Three ways out

When a file stops fitting, you have three honest options:

1. **Use less of it.** Sample it, or filter it down outside R (with
   command-line tools, or by asking whoever sent it for a narrower
   extract). Fine for exploration; not fine when the answer needs all the
   rows.
2. **Put it in a database.** Postgres, SQL Server, DuckDB. The data lives
   somewhere that isn't your RAM, and you send queries to it. This is the
   right answer for a lot of shops, and if yours already has a database,
   use it.
3. **Keep it in files, but stop reading all of it.** Use a file format
   that stores its own types and statistics, and an engine that reads
   only the columns and rows your query actually touches.

This part is about option three, because it needs no server, no DBA
ticket, and no permissions — just a package and a folder. In R, that
package is **arrow**.

## Enter arrow

[Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/) is a specification for how
tabular data is laid out in memory, plus a query engine that works on it.
The `arrow` R package gives you both, and — the part that matters for
you — it speaks `dplyr`.

```{r}
#| label: install-arrow
#| eval: false
pak::pak("arrow")
```

```{r}
#| label: load-arrow
library(arrow)
```

The pivot is one function. Instead of `read_csv()`, which *reads*, use
`open_dataset()`, which **opens**:

```{r}
#| label: open-dataset
lab_ds <- open_dataset(
  book_data_path("synthetic-covid-lab-results.csv"),
  format = "csv"
)

lab_ds
```

Notice what came back. Not a tibble — a **Dataset**: a description of
what's in the file and where, holding no rows at all.

```{r}
#| label: dataset-class
class(lab_ds)
```

`open_dataset()` returned in a fraction of a second and will return just
as fast against a ten-gigabyte file, because it did not read the data —
it read enough of the file to work out its shape and then stopped. What
you're holding is a handle: a path, plus a **schema**, arrow's record of
what every column is.

```{r}
#| label: schema
lab_ds$schema
```

Read that schema carefully, because it is arrow's *guess*. It sampled the
file and inferred those types, exactly as `read_csv()` did — and it made
exactly the same call on `result_snomed`, `specimen_source_snomed`,
`ordering_provider_npi`, and `patient_zip` — all four come back as
`int64` — for exactly the same reason: the CSV doesn't say. Two different tools, same missing information, same
wrong answer. That is not a `readr` problem or an arrow problem. It is a
CSV problem.

You can override it here too, by handing `open_dataset()` a schema
instead of letting it guess — but that means writing out all
forty-three columns, or maintaining a partial schema that has to be kept
in step with the file. Hold that thought.

## Lazy is the whole trick

Write the same positivity pipeline against the Dataset. It looks almost
identical, right up until the last line:

```{r}
#| label: lazy-query
positivity_query <-
  lab_ds |>
  filter(!is.na(specimen_collection_dt)) |>
  mutate(
    collection_date = as.Date(specimen_collection_dt),
    is_positive = result_snomed %in% c("260373001", "10828004")
  ) |>
  group_by(collection_date, test_method) |>
  summarise(tests = n(), positives = sum(is_positive), .groups = "drop")

positivity_query
```

No data. `dplyr` verbs on a Dataset don't compute anything — they
**record what you asked for**. This is *lazy evaluation*, the same idea
behind `dbplyr` sending SQL off to a database: build the whole request
first, run it once, at the end.

`collect()` is the "now actually do it" button:

```{r}
#| label: collect
positivity <-
  positivity_query |>
  collect() |>
  mutate(positivity = round(100 * positives / tests, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(collection_date))

head(positivity, 5)
```

Only now does anything get read. And arrow reads the *minimum* it can:
four columns out of forty-three, because that's all the query mentions.
On a ten-gigabyte file that alone is most of the win — and what lands in
your session is a few hundred rows of summary, not sixteen million rows
of raw feed.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The rule of thumb

Put `collect()` **as late as possible** — after every `filter()`,
`select()`, and `summarise()` you can. Everything before it happens in
arrow, on data that never enters your R session. Everything after it
happens in R, on data that does.

The classic beginner mistake is to `collect()` first and `filter()`
after. That reads the whole file into memory and *then* throws most of it
away — you've done all the work you were trying to avoid.
:::

## What arrow won't do

arrow's engine implements a large subset of `dplyr` and several hundred R
functions, but not all of them. When it meets something it can't
translate, it says so — and falls back to pulling the data into R so that
plain R can finish the job.

That fallback is a correctness feature and a performance trap at the same
time. Your answer is right; your memory savings are gone. Treat any
message about a query being pulled into R as "this query needs
restructuring," not as noise.

Two escape hatches, in order of preference.

**Aggregate first, fuss later.** Nine times out of ten the unsupported
function is being applied to something you were about to summarise
anyway. Do the aggregation in arrow, `collect()` the small result, and do
the fussy part in R where everything works:

```{r}
#| label: aggregate-then-fuss
lab_ds |>
  group_by(performing_lab) |>
  summarise(tests = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  collect() |>
  mutate(
    lab_short = stringr::str_remove(
      performing_lab,
      " (Laboratory|Clinical Lab|of New England).*$"
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(tests))
```

**Hand the query to DuckDB.** `to_duckdb()` passes an arrow Dataset to
the DuckDB engine without copying the data, and DuckDB is a full SQL
engine — window functions, complex joins, the lot. You stay in `dplyr`
the whole way:

```{r}
#| label: to-duckdb
#| eval: false
# "How many people were first-time testers?" needs a window function,
# which arrow's own engine will not do — but DuckDB will.
lab_ds |>
  to_duckdb() |>
  group_by(patient_id) |>
  window_order(specimen_collection_dt) |>
  mutate(test_number = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(test_number == 1) |>
  summarise(first_time_testers = n()) |>
  collect()
```

## Try it at scale

Everything above ran against a 25,000-row file, where none of it
mattered. To feel the difference you need a big one. The generator that
built this dataset takes a row count:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
# from a clone of the book's repo
Rscript data-raw/make-synthetic-lab-results.R --rows 5000000 --out data/scale/big.csv
```

No clone handy? Manufacture one from the file you already have by
appending it to itself. This writes to disk without ever holding the big
version in memory:

```{r}
#| label: make-big-file
#| eval: false
big_path <- here::here("data", "raw", "lab-results-big.csv")
one_copy <- read_csv(here::here("data", "raw", "synthetic-covid-lab-results.csv"))

# The first copy carries the header; the other 199 don't.
write_csv(one_copy, big_path)
for (i in 1:199) {
  write_csv(one_copy, big_path, append = TRUE)
}

fs::file_size(big_path)
```

Five million rows, about three gigabytes. Now run the same two pipelines
against it — `read_csv()` then `dplyr`, versus `open_dataset()` then
`collect()` — and watch what each one does to your machine. The arrow
version will finish. Depending on your laptop, the `read_csv()` version
may not.

## What we fixed, and what we didn't

Reading a CSV lazily beats reading it eagerly. But look again at the four
reasons the wall exists, and notice that **arrow only really solved the
first one**. It reads fewer columns now — but it is still parsing text,
still guessing types, and still unable to answer "how many rows?" without
walking the whole file.

The container is still a CSV. The next chapter changes the container.

::: {.callout-note}
## Where this leaves the brief

You can now compute test positivity *by method* from the lab feed —
something the town-level table could never separate. Hold onto that
pipeline; the project chapter puts it in the Commissioner's brief.
:::
